runs.analysis: A (15 items) is plan-specific and ties into earlier stages, but many of its "adaptation triggers" are copied risk-consequence descriptions rather than measurable monitoring thresholds. Examples are "Seismic event exceeding M5.5-6.5 (10% probability in 20 years) causing €3-8 billion…" and "decommissioning costs estimated to exceed €5-15 billion". The 5/10/15% budget trigger is repeated across items. A omits ethics/anti-corruption, security/cyber and a risk-register review item, and folds climate into corrosion. B (17 items) covers all of A's topics plus those gaps. Its triggers are mostly operational and measurable: SPI/CPI below 0.95, a milestone delay over 2 weeks, turnover above 15%, a tranche delayed more than 4 weeks, yard utilization above 85%, and sea level rise more than 0.1 m above projection. Roles are more specific, and the gauge facts are correct. B's weaknesses are that some frequency fields are one-off completion windows, some thresholds are invented (1 in 10,000 transits), some triggers are qualitative, and it has fewer euro-impact figures. Overall B is more complete and more decision-useful for downstream planning.

Candidate A has 17 monitoring areas, including ethics, security/cyber and climate, which B omits. Its triggers are measurable and operational (SPI/CPI < 0.95 for two months, a delay over 2 weeks, turnover over 15%, yard utilisation over 85%, a tranche delay over 4 weeks). Frequencies and responsible roles are specific, and the content is grounded in the plan (rail gauges, the €250M drawdown threshold, 70% hedging, the 5/10/15% escalation triggers). Weaknesses are some invented or inconsistent thresholds (8% vs 15% contingency), overlap between the finance and funding items, and length. Candidate B is competent and consistent with the governance bodies, and it adds useful construction-platform and buoyancy items. But many of its triggers are risk-register impact figures (e.g. "causing €3-8 billion in repairs") rather than observable monitoring thresholds. Its frequencies are vaguer, it has coverage gaps (no ethics, security, or standalone climate item), and several items name only the PMO or TAG as responsible. A is more complete and more decision-useful.

Candidate A has six tidy items tied to upstream decisions (60% tenant threshold, Decision 4, Critical Risk 3 and 5, RCAB/PSC/CPMG roles). It leaves out PUE and cooling, budget and FX variance, brownfield remediation, fiber and latency, and water. Several triggers are vague ("any official communication from RTE," "failure to receive sign-off"). Item 5 is muddled ("below 40% of ... (60% threshold)"). It also uses 60% where the prompt says 30–50% of the next tranche. Candidate B has eleven items covering all the plan's major risk areas, including grid, tenants, land, security, PUE, social license, brownfield, fiber, finance and FX, the risk register, and phase gates. Many of its triggers are quantified and decision-useful: RTE silence for six months, upgrades above €2B or lead times above three years, a binding allocation 18 months before FID, a 20% remediation overrun, a >10% budget variance, and kill-criteria triggers. It has flaws. "€128.8 km² buffer" is a typo. The local-hire thresholds (75% mandate, 50%, 60%) and the tenant thresholds (30% vs 60%) are inconsistent. A latency target under 1 ms to Paris is doubtful. The brownfield example is confusing. Even so, B is much more complete, specific and useful downstream, and it fits the prompt's skeptical stance better.

Candidate A is much more complete and decision-useful. It has 11 monitoring areas: grid, tenants, land, security, PUE/cooling, social license/workforce, brownfield, fiber, finance/FX, risk register, and phase gates. These match the plan's critical success factors and major risks. Each area has concrete tools, frequencies, responsible roles, escalation paths, and quantified triggers. Examples are RTE silence for 6 months, a grid upgrade over €2B, tenant commitment under 40% by Month 30, PUE over 1.20 for more than 2 weeks, remediation cost overrun above 20%, and a 10% EUR/USD move. It also ties into the escalation matrix, the RCAB veto, and the kill criteria, and it separates EUR and USD exposure and hedging as the prompt requires. It has flaws. There is a typo ("€128.8 km² buffer"). Some thresholds are inconsistent, such as local hire below 50% versus 60%, and tenant gates at 30% and 60%. A few figures look invented, such as €75k/ha. It is also verbose and somewhat repetitive. Even so, it covers the required monitoring ground far better.

Candidate B is concise and ties back to earlier-stage artifacts, such as Review Issues, the Decision 4 threshold, and the Security Separation Report. It is too thin, with only 6 items. It omits financial and FX monitoring, brownfield and environmental compliance, fiber and latency, PUE and cooling performance, and a risk-register review. Several items give only vague tools and triggers, and frequencies are sparse ("Quarterly"). Some adaptation processes are odd, such as the "Power Readiness Lockout Clause" and reclassifying 50% of the ecological buffer to reduce holding costs. That second idea conflicts with the permanent-buffer intent and the social-license posture. It is less useful for downstream planning.

Both candidates use the expected structure (approach, tools, frequency, responsible role, adaptation process, trigger) and refer to the same governance bodies (TASG, OMG, CLAB, PSC) and decisions. Neither can be checked against the upstream documents, so I judged on plausibility and internal consistency.

Candidate A has 6 items. It is concise and mostly consistent. Its triggers are sometimes loose or inconsistent. In item 2 the process says two consecutive cycles, while the trigger says 7 consecutive days. Item 3 gives no time window for "three strikes". Item 5's trigger of "royalties deviating more than 5% from expected" is vague. Its main gap is that it does not monitor the plan's headline success metrics: the 40% through-ticket share, modal shift away from air, and distributor complaints (only a passing mention in item 6). It also has no monitoring of reduction cards, PRM, capacity building or stakeholder resistance. It is decision-useful but narrow on critical success factors.

Candidate B has 11 items. It covers the timeline, clearing and float, enforcement, backstop, and adoption and modal shift (the key success criteria). It also covers commercial terms, PRM, governance agility, capacity grants, political resistance, and reduction cards. Triggers are quantified (8% adoption by Year 1, >15% month-on-month, >25% of float, 95% PRM success), and it ties each item to specific decisions and risks. Some weaknesses:
- It is long, and some thresholds look invented, such as the 8% in Year 1 and the 10% re-work figure.
- Item 2 has a minor inconsistency. It lists a €200M baseline float alongside a "150% of peak daily obligation" rule and a "T+3 fails" trigger, though these may all come from upstream assumptions.
- A "spreadsheet" is a weak tool for €200M of float.
- The "T+5 minutes" label is a slight confusion with A's "T+5", which is probably a minute-level latency figure.

Overall, B covers the project's critical success factors and risks much more completely, and it has clearer and more measurable triggers. This is what the stage requires, and it is more useful downstream. B's length is justified by that coverage.

Candidate A is far more complete and decision-useful. It covers 11 monitoring areas, including the plan's headline goals (40% through-ticket share, complaints halved, modal shift), PRM accessibility, reduction cards, capacity-building grants, and stakeholder resistance. Each item has multiple concrete tools, graded frequencies, named roles, specific adaptation steps, and quantitative triggers. These tie into the earlier governance stages (PSC, OMG, TASG, CLAB, and the decisions and risks they reference).

A has weaknesses. It uses some invented figures: the 5% royalty cap, €900M capacity-building allocation, and 8% Year 1 adoption. Some tools are generic, such as a "Spreadsheet" used as a monitoring tool. It also has small inconsistencies, such as the 95% uptime threshold against the 90% target elsewhere, and some "strikes" definitions that are a bit muddled. Many of these figures appear to derive from the assumptions and decisions in earlier stages, so they are probably not unfaithful. It also gives monitoring of the bicycle, ferry and air hooks no attention, but B does not either.

Candidate B is thin: 6 items, 1–2 tools each, and vague triggers. Examples are "2 calibration weeks" and "T+90 threshold", which is odd given the 90-minute threshold. Its commercial terms trigger ("royalties deviating more than 5%") is muddled. It omits the core success metrics (40% adoption, modal shift), accessibility, reduction cards, capacity building, and stakeholder risk. Its item 3 has a mild inconsistency, since monitoring covers "primary participants" only, and it leaves out the PRM and adoption tracking that the plan's success criteria need. B is concise and consistent but under-covers the stage's purpose of monitoring critical success factors.

Overall A is clearly better.

Candidate A is far more comprehensive. It has 10 monitoring items. They cover gate and budget, operational KPIs, GDPR, health system signals, equity, home interventions, staffing and safety, alert accuracy, health outcomes and the risk register. Each item has concrete tools, frequencies, owners, adaptation processes and quantifiable triggers. It also covers areas the plan prompt requires and B skips: alert trigger calibration, outcome and mortality monitoring, equity by deprivation index, volunteer and staff safety, and multilingual coverage. Its weaknesses are some internal inconsistencies. The early-warning thresholds in item 2 (95% of target, 76% utilization) sit awkwardly beside the 80% gate, and item 2 uses a 75% threshold in one place and 76% in another. There is some verbosity and overlap between items. It also uses "Third-party evaluator" and "Finance Director" roles that may not appear in the earlier governance stages. Even so, it is decision-useful and well-tied to the plan.

Candidate B is concise, but it is thin. It has 6 items, and several have minimal tools and vague triggers, such as "any procedural deviation from GDPR best practices". It omits outcome metrics, alert accuracy, staffing and safety, and equity beyond home interventions. Some content is specific, such as the MCR 50% threshold and the 50:50 split of contracted installs to vouchers. Its item 5 conflates the triage script IRR with the health data loop. Its item 6 has no "units" for its trigger, and its frequency is limited to M3-M6. Its "5% below" trigger is ambiguous: it could mean percentage points or a relative 5%. It also references "Builder path" and review issues without explanation, though these tie to prior stages. Overall it is less complete for monitoring a 12-month program.

A is better.

Both candidates follow the stage structure (approach, tools, frequency, responsible role, adaptation process, trigger) and reference the same governance entities (COAT, PSC, HRC, MCR). So they appear grounded in the earlier stages.

Candidate A has 6 items. It covers gate KPIs, finance, GDPR, risk register, data loop fidelity and home-intervention equity. It leaves out several things the plan requires: health outcome monitoring (EMS calls, ED visits, mortality), alert trigger accuracy, worker protection, staffing and volunteer safety, multilingual coverage, and equity by age or housing type. Some of its triggers are odd or inconsistent. "5% or more below target" is vague. Applying it to "Center Utilization" confuses utilization with the "hours delivered" gate metric. The "50:50 split" is unclear. Item 5 halts door-knocking whenever IRR drops below 95%, which is extreme. Item 2 says "Weekly (M1-M4); Bi-weekly (M5+)", which is fine.

Candidate B has 10 items and is far more comprehensive. It includes gate tracking, GDPR, health system signals, equity and outreach, home interventions with temperature verification, staffing and safety, alert accuracy and alert fatigue, primary outcomes with baseline comparison, and the risk register. Its triggers are quantified and tied to the plan's metrics. It does have some flaws. Its thresholds are sometimes internally inconsistent: gate target 80%, then "<75%" for utilization in one place and "below 76%" in another. It uses a 95% IRR target in one place and a 90% trigger elsewhere. The 3-year baseline comparison is useful but ignores the noise in heat-season data. It is verbose. The "May–September" monitoring window is plausible given a May start. Even so, it is much more complete and decision-useful for this heat plan, and it covers the safety, health-outcome and equity monitoring that the prompt requires.

Overall B is clearly better.
